title: Hierarchical Prototype Learning for Semantic Segmentation
claim: Models misclassify fine-grained parts by ignoring the whole object, while humans first recognize the object and then its parts.
layout: 4 image panels in a 2x2 grid, legends left, speech bubbles right
description: The left column shows a legend: a cow tree with a cow torso label in red, and a horse tree listing the head, ear, muzzle, torso, neck, leg and tail, each with a color swatch. In the center is a photo of two horses behind a fence. A blue arrow leads right to the model's part-segmentation prediction on the top row. A yellow arrow leads down to a horse-only mask, then right to the human-style segmentation on the bottom row. A red dashed box on the model's prediction marks leg pixels wrongly labeled as cow torso. A white dashed box on the human result marks the correctly labeled horse legs. On the right, a blue robot says 'It is a cow's leg' with a red X. A yellow human says 'That's a horse. It's the horse's leg!' with a green check. The eye goes first to the colored masks and the speech bubbles.
caption: Comparison of semantic segmentation between human and computational model.
abstract: Conventional semantic segmentation methods often fail to distinguish fine-grained parts within the same object because of missing links between part-level cues and object-level semantics. Inspired by how humans recognize objects, which involves first identifying them as a whole and then distinguishing their parts, we propose a hierarchical prototype-based segmentation method called Hierarchical Prototype Segmentation (HiPoSeg). This builds a structured prototype space that captures both abstract object-level representations and detailed part-level features, enabling consistent alignment between levels. HiPoSeg leverages a hierarchical contrastive learning strategy to structure semantic representations across levels, encouraging both intra-level discrimination and cross-level consistency. Experiments on standard benchmarks such as Cityscapes, ADE20K, Mapillary Vistas 2.0, and PASCAL-Part-108 demonstrate that HiPoSeg produces consistent performance improvement with an average gain of +3.07\%p mIoU without any additional inference cost.
